standard_text: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantitative variables. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.

progression.narrative:
A scatter plot turns two columns of measurements into a single picture, and reading that picture is a chain of increasingly precise judgments. First a student has to see that each dot is a PAIR -- one measurement of x and one of y for the same thing -- and grasp the language 'as x increases, y ...'. Once dots are pairs, the first real judgment is DIRECTION: do the dots drift up to the right (positive association), down to the right (negative association), or scatter with no drift at all (no association)? Then comes FORM: does the cloud hug a straight line (linear) or bend along a curve (nonlinear)? Riding alongside direction and form are two local features the standard names by hand -- CLUSTERING (points bunched into groups) and OUTLIERS (a lone point far from the pattern) -- which describe where the data sits, not which way it trends.

The payoff of the standard is putting all of this together IN CONTEXT: constructing a plot from a data table and then describing it in the variables' own words -- 'as temperature rose, hot-chocolate sales fell, roughly in a straight line, with one unusually warm day standing apart.' The arc tops out in argument: analyzing whether a described pattern actually matches a plot, building a plot to match given descriptors, and refusing to slide from 'these two things move together' to 'one causes the other.' The Indiana item spec keeps every association visually obvious and one data set per graph, so the work is always description and interpretation, never a computed statistic.

steps.rationale: Direction is the first observable judgment a scatter plot supports, and the Below-proficiency band asks for exactly it: name the association as positive, negative, or none. It comes first because every later description is built on knowing which way the cloud drifts.

Form is the second axis of description the standard names by hand -- linear versus nonlinear. It sits after direction because a student must first see the drift before deciding whether that drift follows a straight line or a curve.

Clustering and outliers are local features the standard lists explicitly. They form a separate step from direction and form because they describe WHERE the points sit -- bunched or lone -- not which way the data trends.

The Approaching-proficiency band asks students to identify MORE THAN ONE characteristic at once. This synthesis step combines direction, form, and any cluster or outlier into a single full description of the plot.

The At-proficiency heart of the standard: construct a scatter plot from a data table and interpret the pattern IN CONTEXT, stating how the response variable changes as the explanatory variable increases, using the real variable names.

The Above-proficiency band: analyze and critique a described pattern, create a scatter plot to match given descriptors, and separate correlation from causation -- refusing to claim one variable causes the other from association alone.

skills.name: Plot and read an ordered pair (x, y) on a coordinate grid

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point from an ordered pair (x, y) and read the coordinates of a plotted point, moving right for x then up for y.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Where does the point (3, 5) go -- right 3 and up 5, or right 5 and up 3?

skills.i_do_script: Walking directions come in a fixed order: go RIGHT down the hallway first, then UP the stairs -- so 'right 3, up 5' ends somewhere different from 'right 5, up 3'. Every dot on a scatter plot is an ordered pair, and order matters: the FIRST number is x (how far RIGHT) and the SECOND is y (how far UP). Watch me plot (3, 5): I start at the corner, move RIGHT 3, then UP 5, and make my dot there. To read a point that is 4 right and 2 up, I write it as (4, 2) -- x first, y second. The trap is swapping them: (3, 5) and (5, 3) land in completely different places.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the x- and y-coordinates -- moves up for the first number and right for the second
canonical_error.example: To plot (3, 5) the student moves RIGHT 5 and UP 3, landing at (5, 3) instead of (3, 5)
canonical_error.why: The student has not fixed the order of the pair. The first coordinate is always the horizontal (x) move and the second is always the vertical (y) move; reversing them plots a different point and would flip the look of a whole scatter plot.

skills.item_template: An ordered pair to plot, or a described point (so many right, so many up) to name. Short-response fluency bank. (No figure needed -- described in text.)

sample_items.stem: To plot (2, 7), how far right and how far up do you move?
sample_items.answer: Right 2, up 7.

sample_items.stem: A point is 6 to the right and 1 up. Write it as an ordered pair.
Which point is farther to the right: (8, 2) or (3, 9)?
sample_items.answer: (8, 2) -- its x-coordinate 8 is larger.

sample_items.stem: Do (4, 9) and (9, 4) name the same point?
sample_items.answer: No -- order matters; they are different points.

sample_items.stem: For the pair (5, 0), how far up do you move?
sample_items.answer: 0 -- the point sits on the x-axis.

sample_items.stem: A dot is at 3 right and 3 up. Write its ordered pair.

redirect_script.stop: Which number moves you right -- the first or the second?
redirect_script.prompt: Walk BOTH orders on the grid with your finger -- your way and the reverse -- and see that they land on two different dots. Always read the pair in order: FIRST number is the right move (x), SECOND number is the up move (y). Point to each number and say 'right, then up' before you place the dot.
redirect_script.praise: You moved right for the first number and up for the second -- ordered pair done right.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that give a point's horizontal then vertical position.
The first number in a pair; how far right (or left) the point is.
The second number in a pair; how far up (or down) the point is.
Data made of pairs, with two measurements recorded for each item.

next_steps.if_fail: Review plotting points on the coordinate plane (grade 5).

worked_example_script.text: Show two dots made from the SAME two numbers: one dot is right 4, up 2, and the other is right 2, up 4. Same numbers, two different spots -- the order of the walk decides which dot you get.
Write 'Plot (4, 2) and (2, 4). Are they the same point?'
For (4, 2), which number tells you how far right, and which tells you how far up?
(4, 2) is right 4, up 2. (2, 4) is right 2, up 4. Different points -- order matters.
If a student plots both at the same spot, ask 'did you keep x first and y second for each one?'
Your turn: plot (5, 1) and (1, 5) and tell me how they are different.

skills.name: Interpret how y changes as x increases from a table of pairs

prerequisite_skill.description: Order pairs by their x-value and describe whether the y-values increase or decrease as x increases.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: For (5, 10), (1, 4), (3, 7), put them in order of x and say whether y goes up or down.

skills.i_do_script: A list of pairs is just the order someone happened to write them down -- like kids arriving at a door in random order. Before you compare their heights, you line the kids up by age; data works the same way. To see a relationship, I ask 'as x gets bigger, what does y do?' -- but only after I line the pairs up in ORDER of x. Watch (5, 10), (1, 4), (3, 7): jumbled, the y-column reads 10, 4, 7 and looks like nothing. Sorted by x -- (1, 4), (3, 7), (5, 10) -- the y-values climb 4, 7, 10, so y INCREASES as x increases. The rule: sort by x first, then read the y-values in that order to see the direction.

canonical_error.pattern: Describes how y changes by reading the y-column in list order, without first ordering the pairs by x
canonical_error.example: For (5, 10), (1, 4), (3, 7) reads the y-column as 10, 4, 7 and says 'y goes up then down, no pattern,' instead of sorting by x to (1,4),(3,7),(5,10) and seeing y rise
canonical_error.why: Covariation is about how y moves AS x increases, so the pairs must be ordered by x before the y-values are read. Reading y in the order it happens to be listed describes nothing about the relationship between the two variables.

skills.item_template: A short list of pairs given out of order. Student sorts by x and states whether y increases or decreases. Short-response fluency bank. (No figure needed.)

sample_items.stem: Order by x and say what y does: (3, 6), (1, 2), (2, 4).
sample_items.answer: Sorted: (1,2),(2,4),(3,6). y increases as x increases.

sample_items.stem: Order by x and say what y does: (4, 5), (2, 9), (3, 7).
sample_items.answer: Sorted: (2,9),(3,7),(4,5). y decreases as x increases.

sample_items.stem: As x increases in (1, 20), (2, 30), (3, 40), what happens to y?
sample_items.answer: y increases (20, 30, 40).

sample_items.stem: As x increases in (10, 8), (20, 5), (30, 2), what happens to y?
sample_items.answer: y decreases (8, 5, 2).

sample_items.stem: Why must you sort the pairs by x before deciding if y goes up or down?
sample_items.answer: Because the direction is about how y changes AS x grows, so x must be in order first.

sample_items.stem: Order by x: (6, 1), (2, 5), (4, 3). Does y rise or fall?
sample_items.answer: Sorted: (2,5),(4,3),(6,1). y falls as x rises.

redirect_script.stop: Are your pairs in order of x yet?
redirect_script.prompt: Before you decide what y does, line the pairs up from smallest x to largest x. THEN read the y-values in that order and say whether they climb or fall.
redirect_script.praise: You sorted by x first, then read y -- that's how you see the real direction.

vocabulary.definition: Gets larger; the values go up.
Gets smaller; the values go down.
The input variable you read across; the 'as x increases' one.
The output variable whose change you describe as x increases.

next_steps.if_fail: Review reading tables and describing change (grade 6).

worked_example_script.text: Here are three (age, height) pairs written in the order the kids walked in: (4, 8), (1, 2), (3, 6). Does the walk-in order tell us anything about how height changes with age? Line the kids up from youngest to oldest first -- NOW read the heights: what do they do?
Write '(4, 8), (1, 2), (3, 6). As x increases, what does y do?'
What is the first thing we do before reading the y-values?
Sort by x: (1, 2), (3, 6), (4, 8). Now the y-values read 2, 6, 8 -- they climb, so y increases as x increases.
If a student reads y as 8, 2, 6 and says 'no pattern,' ask 'did you put the x-values in order first?'
Your turn: (5, 3), (1, 11), (3, 7) -- order by x and tell me what y does.

skills.name: Identify the type of association shown by a scatter plot as positive, negative, or none
skills.i_do_script: Association is something you SEE -- read the cloud, not the list. The type of association is about DIRECTION: which way the dots drift as I read left to right. If y climbs as x increases, the dots drift up to the right -- a POSITIVE association. If y falls as x increases, the dots drift down to the right -- a NEGATIVE association. If the dots scatter with no up-or-down tendency, there is NO association. Watch the pairs (1, 20), (2, 35), (3, 45), (4, 60), (5, 72): as x grows, y grows the whole way, so this is a positive association. The word 'positive' is about the upward direction, not about the numbers being positive.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses 'positive/negative association' with whether the data VALUES are positive or negative numbers, instead of the DIRECTION of the trend
canonical_error.example: For (1, 88), (2, 74), (3, 60), (4, 46), (5, 32) the data drifts DOWNWARD, but because every value is a large positive number the student calls it a 'positive association'
canonical_error.why: Positive versus negative association describes the DIRECTION the cloud drifts -- up-to-the-right or down-to-the-right -- not the sign of the numbers. As x increases, if y decreases the association is negative no matter how large and positive the numbers are.

skills.item_template: A short list of (x, y) pairs given in text. Student names the association as positive, negative, or none by reading the direction. Multiple choice or short response. (No figure needed.)

sample_items.stem: A data set has the pairs (1, 20), (2, 35), (3, 45), (4, 60), (5, 72). As x increases, y increases. What type of association is this?
sample_items.answer: Positive association.

sample_items.stem: (1, 90), (3, 70), (5, 55), (7, 40): as x increases, y decreases. What type of association?
sample_items.answer: Negative association.

sample_items.stem: Shoe size vs math score: (6, 80), (7, 72), (8, 85), (9, 70), (10, 83) -- no clear up or down trend. What type of association?
sample_items.answer: No association (no correlation).

sample_items.stem: (2, 10), (4, 20), (6, 30), (8, 40): what type of association is this?
sample_items.answer: Positive association.

redirect_script.stop: Positive means the numbers are positive, or the dots go UP?
redirect_script.prompt: Ignore the sign of the numbers. Read left to right: if the dots climb, it's positive; if they fall, it's negative; if there's no drift, it's none. Underline the y-values in x-order and see which way they go.
redirect_script.praise: You judged by the direction of the drift, not the sign of the numbers -- that's the real association.

vocabulary.definition: As one variable increases, the other also increases; the dots drift up to the right.
As one variable increases, the other decreases; the dots drift down to the right.
The dots show no clear upward or downward trend; also called no correlation.
A graph of plotted (x, y) pairs used to show the relationship between two variables.

worked_example_script.text: Plot the pairs as dots before saying anything: (1, 12), (2, 9), (3, 7), (4, 4).
Look at the cloud, not the numbers: as your eye moves left to right, do the dots drift up, drift down, or just scatter?
Write '(1, 12), (2, 9), (3, 7), (4, 4). What type of association?'
As x goes 1, 2, 3, 4, what do the y-values do?
y goes 12, 9, 7, 4 -- it falls as x rises, so the dots drift down to the right: a negative association.
If a student says 'positive because all the numbers are positive,' ask 'do the dots go up or down as we move right?'
Your turn: (1, 5), (2, 15), (3, 25), (4, 35) -- what type of association?

practice_problems.stem: In your own words, what does a 'positive association' look like on a scatter plot?
practice_problems.answer: The dots drift up to the right -- as x increases, y increases.

practice_problems.stem: The pairs (2, 10), (4, 20), (6, 30), (8, 40): as x increases, does y go up or down?
practice_problems.answer: Up -- so this is a positive association.

practice_problems.stem: (1, 90), (3, 70), (5, 55), (7, 40): what type of association is this?
practice_problems.answer: Negative -- as x increases, y decreases.

practice_problems.stem: Shoe size vs math score: (6, 80), (7, 72), (8, 85), (9, 70), (10, 83). What type of association?
practice_problems.answer: No association -- y jumps up and down with no clear direction.
practice_problems.notes: No trend even though the numbers are large and positive.

practice_problems.stem: Dre classified the association of (1, 88), (2, 74), (3, 60), (4, 46), (5, 32). Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Dre wrote: 'Every y-value is a big positive number.'
practice_problems.answer: Dre judged by the sign of the numbers. As x increases (1 to 5), y DECREASES (88 down to 32), so the association is NEGATIVE, not positive. 'Positive' refers to the upward direction, not to positive numbers.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: confusing positive numbers with positive association.

practice_problems.stem: Write a set of four (x, y) pairs that shows a negative association, and explain how you know.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 40), (2, 30), (3, 20), (4, 10). As x increases, y decreases every step, so the association is negative.

practice_problems.stem: Two data sets both have all-positive y-values. One is a positive association and one is negative. What is the real difference between them?
practice_problems.answer: The direction the dots drift: positive drifts up to the right (y grows as x grows); negative drifts down to the right (y shrinks as x grows). The sign of the numbers is irrelevant.

activities.title: Which Way Do the Dots Drift?
materials: Card set of pairs-lists, each a small (x, y) data set
activities.instructions:
1. Before sorting any card, sketch its pairs as dots on a mini grid -- the sort is judged by the CLOUD, not the number list.
1. Sort every card into 'Positive association,' 'Negative association,' or 'No association.'
2. For each card, order the pairs by x and underline whether the y-values climb or fall.
3. Rule check: 'positive' means the dots go UP to the right, not that the numbers are positive.
4. Debrief: find a card whose numbers are all positive but whose association is negative -- explain how.

activities.title: Positive Numbers Aren't a Positive Association
activities.instructions:
1. Read Dre's claim that (1, 88), (2, 74), (3, 60), (4, 46), (5, 32) is 'positive because the numbers are positive.'
2. List the y-values in order of x and draw an arrow showing which way they go.
3. The arrow points down, so name the true association.
4. Write the one-sentence rule: association is about direction, not the sign of the numbers.

content.worked_problem: (1, 88), (2, 74), (3, 60), (4, 46), (5, 32). Dre said 'positive' because all the values are positive numbers.
content.error_step: Dre judged the association by the sign of the numbers instead of the direction of the drift.
content.why: As x increases, y decreases from 88 to 32, so the dots drift down to the right -- a negative association.

strategy_links.why: The positive-numbers-versus-positive-association mix-up is a clean, baitable error; find-and-fix with a direction arrow targets it directly.
Drawing the up-to-the-right or down-to-the-right drift arrow over the plotted points (concrete-representational) makes 'direction' visible before it becomes a label.
Think-pair-share on 'which way do these drift?' surfaces the sign-versus-direction disagreement students need to resolve aloud.

questioning_prompts: As you read left to right, do the dots climb, fall, or neither?
What are the y-values in order of x -- do they go up or down?
Is this positive, negative, or no association, and how do you know?
Could a data set of all-positive numbers still be a negative association?
What would 'no association' look like compared to this?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student confuses positive/negative association with whether the data values are positive or negative numbers.
misconception_redirects.say: Ignore the sign of the numbers. Read left to right: if the dots climb, it's positive; if they fall, it's negative; if there's no drift, it's none. Underline the y-values in x-order and see which way they go.
misconception_redirects.praise: You judged by the direction of the drift, not the sign of the numbers -- that's the real association.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a real but loose upward or downward trend 'no association' because the points are not a perfect line.
misconception_redirects.say: An association can be loose. If the dots still tend to climb or fall overall, it counts. Only say 'no association' when there's truly no up-or-down tendency.
misconception_redirects.praise: You spotted the overall tendency even though the dots weren't perfect -- that's a real association.

quick_checks.look_for: Positive (y climbs as x grows). 'Negative' diagnoses reading the direction backwards; 'none' means the student missed the clear trend.
Negative (y falls as x grows). 'Positive' means the student judged by the positive numbers instead of the downward direction.

sentence_starters: As x increases, y ___, so the dots drift ___ to the right.
This is a ___ association because the y-values ___ as x increases.

worked_solution.stem: A data set has the pairs (1, 20), (2, 35), (3, 45), (4, 60), (5, 72). What type of association is this?

steps.annotation: Read the pairs from smallest x to largest x.
List the response values as x increases.
As x increases, y increases.
Up-to-the-right drift is a positive association.

faded_example.stem: (1, 90), (3, 70), (5, 55), (7, 40). What type of association is this?

steps.annotation: Put the pairs in order of increasing x.
List the y-values as x increases.
Do the y-values increase or decrease as x increases?
Name the association: positive, negative, or none.

skills.name: Classify a scatter plot's association as linear or nonlinear
skills.i_do_script: Once I know the direction, I ask about the SHAPE of the path: is it a straight line (LINEAR) or a curve (NONLINEAR)? A quick test is to look at the steps between the y-values as x goes up by ones. If y changes by about the SAME amount each step, the points follow a straight line -- linear. If the steps keep growing or shrinking, or the data turns around, the points bend into a curve -- nonlinear. Watch (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 10), (4, 20), (5, 38): the steps are +3, +5, +10, +18 -- they keep growing, so the path curves. That's a nonlinear association. Nonlinear does NOT mean 'no association' -- it means a curved pattern.

canonical_error.pattern: Assumes any data with a clear direction is 'linear,' without checking whether the points follow a straight path or bend into a curve
canonical_error.example: For (1, 3), (2, 8), (3, 17), (4, 32), (5, 53) the student sees an upward trend and calls it linear, even though the steps +5, +9, +15, +21 keep growing, so the points curve
canonical_error.why: Linear versus nonlinear is about the SHAPE of the path -- a straight line versus a curve -- not merely whether there is a trend. A rising or falling data set is nonlinear when the steps are unequal or the data turns around; 'nonlinear' is not the same as 'no association.'

skills.item_template: A short list of (x, y) pairs with x increasing by a fixed step. Student judges linear vs nonlinear from whether the y-steps are equal or changing. Multiple choice or short response. (No figure needed.)

sample_items.stem: (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30), (4, 40), (5, 50): is the association linear or nonlinear?
sample_items.answer: Linear -- y goes up by a constant 10 each step, a straight line.
Linear -- y drops by a constant 8 each step (a straight downward line).
Nonlinear -- the steps (+3, +5, +10, +18, +22) keep growing, so the path curves.
Nonlinear -- y falls then rises (a U-shape), so it cannot be a straight line.

redirect_script.stop: Straight line, or a curve -- which shape is it?
redirect_script.prompt: A trend alone doesn't make it linear. Check the steps between the y-values: equal steps = a straight line (linear); steps that grow, shrink, or turn around = a curve (nonlinear).
redirect_script.praise: You checked the shape of the path, not just the direction -- that's how you tell linear from nonlinear.

vocabulary.definition: The points follow a straight-line path; y changes by about the same amount for each equal step in x.
The points bend along a curve; the pattern is not a straight line.
The shape of the pattern in a scatter plot -- straight (linear) or curved (nonlinear).

worked_example_script.text: Write '(1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12), (4, 16). Linear or nonlinear?'
How much does y change from each point to the next?
y goes up by 4 every step -- always the same amount -- so the points sit on a straight line: linear.
If a student calls a curve 'linear' just because it rises, ask 'are the steps the same size, or are they changing?'
Your turn: (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 16) -- linear or nonlinear? Check the steps.

practice_problems.stem: What is the difference between a 'linear' and a 'nonlinear' association?
practice_problems.answer: Linear points follow a straight-line path; nonlinear points bend along a curve.

practice_problems.stem: (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30), (4, 40), (5, 50): do the y-values go up by the same amount each step?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- up 10 each time, so the path is a straight line (linear).
Linear -- y drops by a constant 8 each step, a straight downward line.
Nonlinear -- the steps +3, +5, +10, +18, +22 keep growing, so the path curves.

practice_problems.stem: Priya classified the form of (1, 3), (2, 8), (3, 17), (4, 32), (5, 53). Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Priya wrote: 'The dots go up as x increases.'
'Since it has a clear upward trend, the association is linear.'
practice_problems.answer: Priya checked only the DIRECTION, not the shape. The steps are +5, +9, +15, +21 -- they keep growing, so the points bend along a curve. The association is positive but NONLINEAR, not linear.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: equating 'has a trend' with 'linear.'

practice_problems.answer: Nonlinear -- y falls then rises (a U-shape), so it cannot be a straight line.

practice_problems.stem: Write a list of (x, y) pairs for a NONLINEAR association that still trends generally upward.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 8), (4, 16), (5, 32) -- doubling makes the steps grow, so it curves upward.

practice_problems.stem: A classmate says 'nonlinear means there's no association.' Is that right? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No. Nonlinear data can have a strong association -- the points follow a clear curve. 'No association' means no pattern at all; 'nonlinear' means a curved pattern.

activities.title: Straight or Curved?
materials: Card set of pairs-lists with x increasing by ones
activities.instructions:
1. Sort every card into 'Linear' or 'Nonlinear.'
2. For each card, write the step between each pair of y-values.
3. Rule: equal steps = a straight line; steps that grow, shrink, or turn around = a curve.
4. Debrief: find a nonlinear card that still trends upward, and explain why it is not linear.

activities.title: A Trend Isn't Always a Line
materials: Slip with Priya's 'trend means linear' reasoning
activities.instructions:
1. Read Priya's claim that (1, 3), (2, 8), (3, 17), (4, 32), (5, 53) is linear 'because it goes up.'
2. Write the step between each pair of y-values in a row.
3. Notice the steps keep growing -- that means the path bends.
4. Write the corrected description (positive but nonlinear) and the rule: check the steps, not just the direction.

content.worked_problem: (1, 3), (2, 8), (3, 17), (4, 32), (5, 53). Priya said 'linear because it has an upward trend.'
content.error_step: Priya judged the form by the direction alone, ignoring whether the steps are equal.
content.why: The steps +5, +9, +15, +21 keep growing, so the points curve -- the association is positive but nonlinear.

strategy_links.why: The 'has a trend, so it's linear' error is precise and baitable; find-and-fix that writes out the y-steps corrects it.
Laying a straight edge against the plotted points (concrete-representational) shows whether they hug a line or peel away into a curve.
Thinking aloud 'equal steps = a line, growing steps = a curve' models the exact check students skip.

questioning_prompts: How much does y change from each point to the next -- is it the same amount?
Do the points hug a straight line, or do they bend?
Is the direction positive or negative, AND is the form linear or nonlinear?
Could a set that curves still have a strong association?
How is 'nonlinear' different from 'no association'?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student assumes any data with a clear direction is linear without checking the shape of the path.
misconception_redirects.say: A trend alone doesn't make it linear. Check the steps between the y-values: equal steps = a straight line (linear); steps that grow, shrink, or turn around = a curve (nonlinear).
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the shape of the path, not just the direction -- that's how you tell linear from nonlinear.

misconception_redirects.say: Nonlinear still has a pattern -- it's a curve. 'No association' means no pattern at all. Ask: do the points follow a curve, or scatter with no shape?
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept a curved pattern separate from no pattern -- nonlinear is still an association.

quick_checks.look_for: Linear (constant +6 steps). 'Nonlinear' means the student didn't check that the steps are equal.
Nonlinear (steps +3, +5, +7 grow -- a curve). 'Linear' diagnoses judging by the upward trend instead of the steps.

sentence_starters: The steps between the y-values are ___, so the path is ___.
This association is ___ (linear/nonlinear) because the points ___.

worked_solution.stem: The pairs (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 10), (4, 20), (5, 38), (6, 60) show a clear upward trend. Is the association linear or nonlinear?

steps.annotation: List the y-values in order of x.
Find how much y jumps at each step.

steps.math: the jumps keep GROWING, not staying equal
steps.annotation: A straight line adds the same amount each step; these grow.

steps.math: growing steps => a curved path => NONLINEAR
steps.annotation: The points bend along a curve, so the association is nonlinear.

faded_example.stem: (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30), (4, 40), (5, 50): is the association linear or nonlinear?

steps.annotation: List the y-values as x increases.
Find the change at each step.

skills.name: Identify clustering and outliers in a scatter plot
skills.i_do_script: Picture the dots as kids on a playground: most stand together in a huddle, and sometimes one kid stands way off alone. The huddle and the loner get different names, and the picture tells you which is which. Besides direction and shape, I describe WHERE the points sit. CLUSTERING is when several points bunch tightly together in a group. An OUTLIER is a single point that sits far away from all the others. Watch (1, 10), (2, 12), (3, 11), (4, 13), (20, 80): four of the points are bunched near x = 1 to 4 with y around 10 to 13 -- that bunch is a cluster. The point (20, 80) sits way off by itself -- that lonely point is an outlier. The key difference: a cluster is MANY points close together; an outlier is ONE point far from the rest.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses clustering with outliers -- labels a single far-off point a 'cluster,' or calls a tight bunch of points 'outliers'
canonical_error.example: In (1, 10), (2, 12), (3, 11), (4, 13), (20, 80) the student calls the lone point (20, 80) 'a cluster' and treats the tight bunch near x = 1 to 4 as unremarkable, when it is exactly the reverse
canonical_error.why: Clustering means several points bunched close together; an outlier means one point far from all the others. A cluster is a group of many points; an outlier is a single lonely point. Swapping the two labels describes the plot backwards.

skills.item_template: A short list of (x, y) pairs, most bunched with one or none far off, given in text. Student names the cluster and/or the outlier. Multiple choice or short response. (No figure needed.)

sample_items.answer: (20, 80) -- it sits far from all the others.

sample_items.stem: (5, 5), (5, 6), (6, 5), (6, 7), (7, 6): describe where these points sit.
sample_items.answer: They are clustered -- bunched tightly near x = 5 to 7, y = 5 to 7, with no outlier.

sample_items.stem: (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 4), (18, 40): identify the cluster and the outlier.
sample_items.answer: Cluster: the four points near x = 2 to 5, y = 3 to 4. Outlier: (18, 40).

sample_items.stem: A plot has most points bunched near (10, 10) but one point at (40, 5). Is (40, 5) a cluster or an outlier?
sample_items.answer: An outlier -- it is one point far from the bunched group (which is the cluster).

redirect_script.stop: One lonely point, or a whole bunch -- which are you naming?
redirect_script.prompt: A cluster is MANY points bunched together; an outlier is ONE point far from the rest. Circle the bunch and put a box around any lonely point before you label them.
redirect_script.praise: You called the bunch a cluster and the lone point an outlier -- exactly the right labels.

vocabulary.definition: Several data points bunched closely together in a group.
A single data point that sits far away from all the other points.
A group of points that are close together on the scatter plot.

worked_example_script.text: Plot the five points (2, 20), (3, 22), (2, 21), (3, 23), (15, 60) as plain dots -- no labels yet.
Look at the dots like kids on a playground: which dots are standing in a tight group together? Is any dot standing far off by itself? Circle the group and put a box around the loner.

Four dots huddle together near the left -- MANY points close together, and the group gets the group word: CLUSTER. The single dot way out at (15, 60) stands alone -- ONE point far from the rest, and the loner gets the lone word: OUTLIER.
Which points are bunched together, and is any point off by itself?
Four points bunch near x = 2 to 3, y about 20 to 23 -- that's the cluster. (15, 60) is far away and alone -- that's the outlier.
If a student calls (15, 60) 'a cluster,' ask 'is that one point or a group of points?'
Your turn: (1, 4), (2, 5), (1, 6), (2, 4), (12, 30) -- name the cluster and the outlier.

practice_problems.stem: In your own words, what is an outlier on a scatter plot?
practice_problems.answer: A single point that sits far away from all the other points.

practice_problems.stem: (1, 10), (2, 12), (3, 11), (4, 13), (20, 80): which point is far from the rest?
practice_problems.answer: (20, 80) -- it is the outlier.

practice_problems.stem: (5, 5), (5, 6), (6, 5), (6, 7), (7, 6): describe where these points sit.
practice_problems.answer: They are clustered -- bunched tightly near x = 5 to 7, y = 5 to 7, with no outlier.

practice_problems.stem: (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 4), (18, 40): identify the cluster and the outlier.
practice_problems.answer: Cluster: the four points near x = 2 to 5, y = 3 to 4. Outlier: (18, 40), far from the rest.

practice_problems.stem: Sam described the scatter (1, 10), (2, 12), (3, 11), (4, 13), (20, 80). Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Sam wrote: 'The point (20, 80) is way out by itself.'
practice_problems.answer: Sam mixed up the terms. A CLUSTER is several points bunched together -- that's the group near x = 1 to 4. A single lonely point like (20, 80) is an OUTLIER, not a cluster.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: calling a single far-off point a 'cluster.'

practice_problems.stem: A plot has most points bunched near (10, 10) but one point at (40, 5). Is (40, 5) a cluster or an outlier?
practice_problems.answer: An outlier -- it is one point sitting far from the bunched group (which is the cluster).

practice_problems.stem: Write a set of six (x, y) pairs that has a clear cluster AND one outlier. Label them.
practice_problems.answer: Example: cluster (1, 20), (2, 21), (2, 19), (3, 20), (3, 22); outlier (15, 60). Five points bunch near (1 to 3, about 20); (15, 60) is far away.

practice_problems.stem: Does adding an outlier change whether a data set has a positive or negative association? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: It can distort the look, but the overall direction is judged from the bulk of the points; a single outlier is noted separately and does not by itself define the association.
practice_problems.notes: Connects outliers to the association judgment.

activities.title: Clustered, or Is There an Outlier?
activities.instructions:
1. Sort every card into 'Clustered, no outlier' or 'Has an outlier.'
2. For each card, circle the bunched group and box any lonely point.
3. Rule: a cluster is many points close together; an outlier is one point far away.
4. Debrief: pick a 'has an outlier' card and point to both the cluster and the outlier on it.

activities.title: Is It a Cluster or an Outlier?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Sam's claim that the lone point (20, 80) is 'a cluster.'
2. Circle every point that is bunched with others and box the point that stands alone.
3. Count: a cluster needs many points; a lone point is an outlier.
4. Write the corrected labels and the rule that tells them apart.

content.error_step: Sam labeled a single lonely point as a cluster.
content.why: A cluster is the group of bunched points (x = 1 to 4); the single far-off point (20, 80) is an outlier.

strategy_links.why: The cluster-versus-outlier label swap is a clean, baitable error; find-and-fix that circles the bunch and boxes the lone point corrects it.
Physically circling clusters and boxing outliers on the plotted points (concrete-representational) fixes the vocabulary to the picture.
Think-pair-share on 'is that a cluster or an outlier?' forces students to defend which points are bunched versus lone.

questioning_prompts: Which points are bunched together in a group?
Is any single point sitting far from all the others?
Is that one lonely point, or a whole group of points?
Where is the cluster, and where is the outlier?
Could a plot have a cluster but no outlier?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student confuses clustering with outliers -- calls a single far point a cluster or a tight bunch outliers.
misconception_redirects.say: A cluster is MANY points bunched together; an outlier is ONE point far from the rest. Circle the bunch and put a box around any lonely point before you label them.
misconception_redirects.praise: You called the bunch a cluster and the lone point an outlier -- exactly the right labels.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a point at the high or low end of the trend an outlier even though it still follows the pattern.
misconception_redirects.say: An outlier must be far from the PATTERN, not just at the end of it. A point that still fits the trend is not an outlier.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked whether the point breaks from the pattern before calling it an outlier -- that's the real test.

quick_checks.look_for: Both -- the four bunched points are the cluster and (20, 50) is the outlier. Naming only one means the student missed a feature.
No -- all points are clustered, no outlier. Naming an outlier here means the student flagged an in-pattern point.

sentence_starters: The points near ___ are a cluster because they are ___.
The point ___ is an outlier because it sits ___ from the others.

worked_solution.stem: Describe the scatter (1, 10), (2, 12), (3, 11), (4, 13), (20, 80): is there clustering, an outlier, or both?
worked_solution.answer: Both -- a cluster of four points and one outlier at (20, 80)

skills.name: Describe more than one characteristic of a scatter plot at once
skills.i_do_script: A full description of a scatter plot names MORE THAN ONE thing. I run a short checklist: first the DIRECTION (positive, negative, or none), then the FORM (linear or nonlinear), then any FEATURES (a cluster or an outlier). Watch (1, 20), (2, 30), (3, 42), (4, 55), (5, 66), (20, 15): the bulk of the points climb by about 10 each step, so it's positive and roughly linear -- but (20, 15) sits far below that rising pattern, so there's an outlier too. My description: 'a positive, linear association with an outlier.' One label alone would be incomplete.

canonical_error.pattern: Names only one characteristic -- usually the direction -- and stops, ignoring the plot's other features like form or an outlier
canonical_error.example: For (1, 15), (2, 26), (3, 38), (4, 50), (5, 61), (18, 12) the student says only 'positive association' and never mentions that the bulk is roughly linear or that (18, 12) is an outlier
canonical_error.why: The standard asks students to identify MULTIPLE characteristics at once. A complete description reports direction AND form, and flags any cluster or outlier; naming a single feature under-describes the plot.

skills.item_template: A short list of (x, y) pairs, usually with a clear trend plus an outlier, given in text. Student names two or more characteristics. Multiple choice (select two) or short response. (No figure needed.)

sample_items.answer: A positive, linear association (the bulk) AND an outlier at (20, 15).

sample_items.stem: (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 11), (4, 21), (5, 36): name TWO characteristics of this data.
sample_items.answer: A positive association that is nonlinear -- the steps +3, +6, +10, +15 keep growing.
Negative and linear -- y falls by about 20 each step.

sample_items.stem: A plot's points bunch tightly along a straight downward line with no stray points. Give two characteristics.
sample_items.answer: Negative and linear, with the points clustered along the line and no outliers.

redirect_script.stop: You named one thing -- what else does the plot show?
redirect_script.prompt: Run the whole checklist: direction (positive/negative/none), then form (linear/nonlinear), then features (any cluster or outlier). Give at least two of them for a complete description.
redirect_script.praise: You reported the direction AND the form (and the outlier) -- that's a full description, not just one label.

vocabulary.definition: A feature of a scatter plot: its direction, its form, or a cluster or outlier.
Whether the association is positive, negative, or none.
The overall relationship a scatter plot shows between the two variables.

worked_example_script.text: Plot the six points first: (1, 20), (2, 30), (3, 42), (4, 55), (5, 66), and the stray (20, 15).
Run the checklist on the PICTURE: which way does the bulk drift? Does it climb like a line or bend? And what is that lone dot doing way out at (20, 15)?
Write '(1, 8), (2, 16), (3, 24), (4, 32), (15, 6). Name two characteristics.'
What is the direction? What is the form? Is anything off by itself?
The bulk climbs by 8 each step -- positive and linear. But (15, 6) sits far below the trend -- an outlier. So: positive, linear, with an outlier.
If a student says only 'positive,' ask 'is that everything? What about the shape and that lonely point?'
Your turn: (1, 50), (2, 40), (3, 30), (4, 20), (5, 10) -- name two characteristics.

practice_problems.stem: Name the two things a full description of a scatter plot's overall trend should include.
practice_problems.answer: The direction (positive/negative/none) AND the form (linear/nonlinear) -- plus any outliers or clusters.
Negative and linear -- y falls by about 20 each step.
A positive, linear association (the bulk) AND an outlier at (20, 15).

practice_problems.stem: (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 11), (4, 21), (5, 36): name TWO characteristics of this data.
practice_problems.answer: A positive association that is nonlinear (curved) -- the steps +3, +6, +10, +15 keep growing.

practice_problems.stem: Lena was asked for TWO characteristics of (1, 15), (2, 26), (3, 38), (4, 50), (5, 61), (18, 12). Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Lena wrote: 'The data has a positive association.'
practice_problems.answer: Lena named only ONE characteristic and stopped. The question asks for more than one: the bulk is positive AND roughly linear, and there is an OUTLIER at (18, 12) far below the trend. A full description reports at least two features.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: naming one characteristic and stopping.

practice_problems.stem: A scatter plot's points bunch tightly along a straight downward line with no stray points. Give two characteristics.
practice_problems.answer: Negative and linear, with the points clustered along the line and no outliers.

practice_problems.stem: Write a set of (x, y) pairs and then list EVERY characteristic it shows.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 10), (2, 18), (3, 27), (4, 35), (5, 44), (12, 8). Characteristics: positive, linear association with an outlier at (12, 8).

practice_problems.stem: Two students describe the same plot. One says 'positive.' The other says 'positive, linear, with one outlier.' Which is the better answer for this standard, and why?
practice_problems.answer: The second -- the standard asks students to describe patterns such as direction, form, and outliers. Naming multiple characteristics gives a complete description.

activities.title: Match the Plot to Its Full Description
materials: Description cards naming two or more characteristics
activities.instructions:
1. Match each data-list card to the description that names ALL of its characteristics.
2. Before claiming a match, say the direction, the form, and any outlier out loud.
3. Set aside the decoy descriptions that name only one feature or the wrong one.
4. Debrief: why is a one-word description not enough for this standard?

activities.title: One Word Isn't Enough
activities.instructions:
1. Read Lena's answer 'positive association' for (1, 15), (2, 26), (3, 38), (4, 50), (5, 61), (18, 12).
2. Run the checklist: direction, then form, then features.
3. Add the characteristics Lena missed (the linear form and the outlier at (18, 12)).
4. Write the complete description and the rule: name at least two characteristics.

content.error_step: Lena named one characteristic and stopped.
content.why: The bulk is positive and roughly linear, and (18, 12) is an outlier -- a full description names more than one.

strategy_links.why: Gradual release of a 'direction / form / features' checklist (I-do, we-do, you-do) builds the habit of naming more than one characteristic.
The 'named one thing and stopped' error is baitable; find-and-fix that lists the missed features corrects the under-description.
Think-pair-share on 'what else does this plot show?' pushes students past their first single label.

questioning_prompts: What is the direction -- positive, negative, or none?
What is the form -- linear or nonlinear?
Is there a cluster or an outlier to mention?
You gave one characteristic -- what else is true about this plot?
How many characteristics does a complete description need here?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student names only one characteristic (usually the direction) and stops.
misconception_redirects.say: Run the whole checklist: direction (positive/negative/none), then form (linear/nonlinear), then features (any cluster or outlier). Give at least two of them for a complete description.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reported the direction AND the form (and the outlier) -- that's a full description, not just one label.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student flags an outlier that actually still fits the trend, or repeats the direction twice as two 'characteristics.'
misconception_redirects.say: Each checklist item is a different question: direction, form, and features. Make sure your two characteristics answer two different questions.
misconception_redirects.praise: You gave two DIFFERENT characteristics -- direction and form -- not the same idea twice.

quick_checks.look_for: Positive and linear WITH an outlier at (14, 3). Naming only 'positive' diagnoses stopping at one characteristic.
Positive and nonlinear (steps +4, +8, +16 grow). Answering 'positive, linear' means the student skipped the form check.

sentence_starters: This plot is ___ (direction) and ___ (form), and it also has ___.
Two characteristics of this data are ___ and ___.

worked_solution.stem: Name TWO characteristics of the scatter (1, 20), (2, 30), (3, 42), (4, 55), (5, 66), (20, 15).
worked_solution.answer: A positive, linear association AND an outlier at (20, 15)

steps.math: main points (x = 1 to 5): y = 20, 30, 42, 55, 66 rise by about 10 each
steps.annotation: The bulk climbs steadily -- a positive, roughly linear trend.

steps.math: rising by a near-equal amount => positive and linear
steps.annotation: Equal-size upward steps mean a linear, positive association.

steps.math: (20, 15) sits far below the rising pattern
steps.annotation: One point breaks away from the trend -- an outlier.

steps.annotation: Report both features, not just one.
List the y-values in order of x.
Find the change at each step.

skills.name: Construct a scatter plot from a table and interpret the pattern in context
skills.i_do_script: Here I turn a data table into a plot and then say what it means using the REAL variable names. The first column is x (the explanatory variable) and the second is y (the response). Watch a table of temperature (F) and bottled waters sold: (60, 15), (70, 22), (80, 30), (90, 41), (100, 52). I plot each pair, then read the direction: as temperature goes up, sales go up, so it's a positive association. In context: 'As temperature increases, the number of waters sold increases.' The key move is to track the RESPONSE variable as the explanatory variable grows -- and to say it in the story's own words.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the contextual direction backwards -- reports the response variable increasing when the plot shows it decreasing (or the reverse) as x increases
canonical_error.example: For a plot of years (x) versus town population (y) whose dots fall from left to right, the student completes 'As time increased, the population INCREASED,' when the points show population decreasing
canonical_error.why: Interpreting in context means tracking the response variable's direction as x grows. Falling dots mean y DECREASES as x increases -- a negative association -- so the contextual sentence must say 'decreased.' Naming the wrong direction misreports the relationship.

skills.item_template: A data table (given as text pairs) with named variables. Student states the association and completes an in-context sentence, or plots the points. Multiple part (construct + interpret). (Data shown as a table/pairs in text; no scatter figure invented.)

sample_items.stem: Temperature (F) vs bottled waters sold: (60, 15), (70, 22), (80, 30), (90, 41), (100, 52). Complete: 'As temperature increases, sales ___.' What is the association?
sample_items.answer: increase; a positive association.

sample_items.stem: Years since 2000 vs town population (hundreds): (0, 50), (5, 44), (10, 38), (15, 30), (20, 22). Complete: 'As time increased, the population ___.'
sample_items.answer: decreased -- a negative association.

sample_items.stem: Miles driven vs gas remaining (gal): (0, 12), (50, 10), (100, 7), (150, 5), (200, 2). Describe the pattern in context.
sample_items.answer: Negative: as miles driven increase, gas remaining decreases (roughly linear).

sample_items.stem: Hours studied vs test score: (1, 55), (2, 62), (3, 70), (4, 78), (5, 85). Interpret the pattern in context.
sample_items.answer: Positive: as hours studied increase, test scores increase (roughly linear).

redirect_script.stop: Do the dots go up or down as you read right?
redirect_script.prompt: Track the response variable as x increases: if the dots fall, the response DECREASES; if they rise, it INCREASES. Then fill the in-context sentence to match the direction of the dots.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the sentence to the direction of the dots -- that's interpreting in context correctly.

vocabulary.definition: Plot the (x, y) pairs from a data table to make a scatter plot.
Describe the pattern using the real variable names and what they mean.
Stated in terms of the actual quantities, such as temperature and sales.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Hours of daylight vs ice-cream sales: (10, 20), (12, 28), (14, 35), (16, 44). Interpret in context.'
As the hours of daylight increase, what do the sales do?
Sales go 20, 28, 35, 44 as daylight increases -- they rise. In context: as daylight hours increase, ice-cream sales increase. That's a positive association.
If a student writes 'sales decrease,' ask 'are the sales numbers getting bigger or smaller as daylight goes up?'
Your turn: temperature vs hot-cocoa sales (30, 50), (40, 40), (50, 30), (60, 20) -- interpret in context.

practice_problems.stem: When you plot a table of (temperature, sales) pairs, which value goes on the x-axis?
practice_problems.answer: The first/explanatory variable -- temperature goes on the x-axis, sales on the y-axis.

practice_problems.stem: A plot of hours studied vs test score drifts upward. Complete: 'As hours studied increase, test scores ___.'
practice_problems.answer: increase (a positive association).

practice_problems.stem: Temperature (F) vs bottled waters sold: (60, 15), (70, 22), (80, 30), (90, 41), (100, 52). Describe the pattern in context.
practice_problems.answer: Positive association: as temperature increases, water sales increase (roughly linear).

practice_problems.stem: Years since 2000 vs town population (hundreds): (0, 50), (5, 44), (10, 38), (15, 30), (20, 22). Complete: 'As time increased, the population ___.'
practice_problems.answer: decreased -- a negative association.

practice_problems.stem: A store tracked temperature (F) and hot-cocoa cups sold: (30, 50), (40, 42), (50, 33), (60, 25), (70, 16). Jo interpreted it. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Jo wrote: 'The dots on my plot go down from left to right.'
'So as temperature increases, cocoa sales INCREASE.'
practice_problems.answer: Jo read the direction backwards. Falling dots mean the response DECREASES as x increases: as temperature increases, cocoa sales DECREASE. It is a negative association.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: reading the contextual direction backwards.

practice_problems.stem: Plot these and describe: miles driven vs gas remaining (gal): (0, 12), (50, 10), (100, 7), (150, 5), (200, 2). What is the association, in context?
practice_problems.answer: Negative: as miles driven increase, gas remaining decreases (roughly linear).

practice_problems.stem: Make a small table (5 pairs) for 'practice hours vs free-throw %' that shows a positive association, then interpret it in context.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 40), (2, 48), (3, 55), (4, 63), (5, 70). As practice hours increase, free-throw percentage increases -- a positive association.

practice_problems.stem: A plot of 'shoe size vs test score' shows dots scattered with no upward or downward drift. Write the correct in-context interpretation.
practice_problems.answer: There is no association: as shoe size increases, test scores do not consistently increase or decrease.

activities.title: Plot It, Then Say It
activities.instructions:
1. Take a table card, label the x-axis with the first variable and the y-axis with the second.
2. Plot every pair to build the scatter plot.
3. Read the direction of the dots and fill the sentence frame: 'As ___ increases, ___ ___.'
4. Debrief: swap plots with another pair and check that their sentence matches the direction of their dots.

content.error_step: A pair labels the axes but writes 'sales decrease' though the dots rise.
content.why: The dots climb as temperature increases, so the in-context sentence must say sales increase -- a positive association.

activities.title: Which Way Do the Dots Really Go?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jo's claim that falling dots mean 'sales increase' for temperature vs cocoa sales.
2. List the sales values in order of temperature and draw an arrow for their direction.
3. The arrow points down, so fix the sentence to say 'decrease.'
4. Write the rule: the in-context sentence must match the direction of the dots.

content.worked_problem: Temperature vs cocoa cups: (30, 50), (40, 42), (50, 33), (60, 25), (70, 16). Jo said 'as temperature increases, sales increase.'
content.error_step: Jo named the wrong direction -- the dots fall, but Jo wrote 'increase.'
content.why: As temperature rises, cocoa sales fall from 50 to 16, so the association is negative: sales DECREASE.

strategy_links.why: Moving from table to plotted points to an in-context sentence (concrete-representational-abstract) anchors the interpretation to the picture the student built.
The backwards-direction interpretation is a clean, baitable error; find-and-fix with a direction arrow corrects it.
A math-journal sentence in the variables' own words consolidates 'interpret in context' as a writing habit.

questioning_prompts: Which variable goes on the x-axis, and which on the y-axis?
As x increases, do the plotted points rise or fall?
Say the pattern using the real variable names, not just 'x and y.'
Does your sentence match the direction of the dots?
Is this a positive, negative, or no association in context?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads the contextual direction backwards -- says the response increases when the dots fall (or the reverse).
misconception_redirects.say: Track the response variable as x increases: if the dots fall, the response DECREASES; if they rise, it INCREASES. Then fill the in-context sentence to match the direction of the dots.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the sentence to the direction of the dots -- that's interpreting in context correctly.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots the table with the axes swapped, putting the response on the x-axis.
misconception_redirects.say: The explanatory variable -- the 'as ___ increases' one -- goes on the x-axis; the response goes on the y-axis. Label the axes before you plot.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put the explanatory variable on x and the response on y -- the plot now tells the right story.

quick_checks.prompt: Hours of sleep vs number of yawns: (8, 1), (6, 4), (4, 7), (2, 10). Interpret in context.
quick_checks.look_for: As hours of sleep increase, yawns decrease (negative). Saying 'yawns increase' diagnoses reading the direction backwards.

quick_checks.prompt: Age (yr) vs height (in): (5, 42), (7, 48), (9, 53), (11, 58). Interpret in context.
quick_checks.look_for: As age increases, height increases (positive). A swapped or 'decrease' answer signals a direction or axis error.

skills.name: Analyze and critique claims about association, and build a plot to match descriptors
skills.i_do_script: At the top of this standard I ARGUE about scatter plots: I judge whether a described pattern really matches the data, I build a plot to fit given descriptors, and I refuse to jump from 'these move together' to 'one causes the other.' Watch a claim: a plot shows a strong positive association between the number of firefighters sent to a fire and the damage caused, and a student says 'more firefighters CAUSE more damage.' The plot really does show a positive association -- but a scatter plot shows only that two things move TOGETHER, never that one causes the other. A hidden variable, the fire's SIZE, drives both. So the honest description is 'a positive association,' and the causal claim is not justified.

canonical_error.pattern: Concludes that because two variables show an association, one must CAUSE the other -- treating correlation as causation
canonical_error.example: A positive association between ice-cream sales (x) and sunburns (y) leads the student to claim 'buying ice cream causes sunburns,' ignoring that hot, sunny weather drives both
canonical_error.why: An association shows the variables move together, not that one produces the other. A hidden (confounding) variable can drive both, so a scatter plot alone can describe a pattern but cannot establish causation.

skills.item_template: A described scatter plot (as text pairs or a described pattern) plus a claim, or a set of descriptors to build a plot for. Student critiques the claim, repairs a description, or lists points matching descriptors. Multiple-part short response. (No scatter figure invented; data shown as text pairs.)

sample_items.stem: A plot shows a strong positive association between the number of firefighters at a fire and the damage caused. A student says 'more firefighters cause more damage.' Is the claim justified?
sample_items.answer: No. A scatter plot shows association, not causation. Bigger fires cause both more firefighters AND more damage.

sample_items.stem: Create a set of (x, y) pairs (at least 6 points) with a negative, linear association and one outlier. List them.
A person's plot rises and then bends upward more steeply, and they call it 'positive, linear.' Correct the description.
sample_items.answer: The direction (positive) is right, but the form is wrong: a bending path is nonlinear. It is a positive, nonlinear association.

sample_items.stem: True or false: a scatter plot with a positive association proves that x causes y.
sample_items.answer: False -- association does not prove causation.

redirect_script.stop: Move together, or one CAUSES the other -- which does the plot show?
redirect_script.prompt: A scatter plot can only show that two things move together. Before claiming cause, ask 'could a hidden variable explain both?' If yes, say the variables are associated, not that one causes the other.
redirect_script.praise: You named the pattern as an association and questioned the cause -- that's honest analysis.

vocabulary.definition: An association means two variables move together; causation means one makes the other change -- a scatter plot shows only association.
A hidden third variable that influences both plotted variables.
Judge whether a claim about the data is justified and explain why or why not.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for line of best fit, bivariate patterns, and two-way tables (8.DSP.2-4, AI.DS.4).

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Positive association between hours of TV and shoe size in kids. Claim: watching TV grows your feet.'
Is there really a cause here, or could something else explain both?
Older kids watch more TV AND have bigger feet -- AGE drives both. The plot shows an association, but TV does not cause bigger feet. Correlation is not causation.
If a student accepts the causal claim, ask 'what hidden variable could be behind both?'
Your turn: critique 'more lifeguards on duty causes more drownings' when the two are positively associated.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: if two variables have a positive association, then one must cause the other.
practice_problems.answer: False -- association is not the same as causation.

practice_problems.stem: Rewrite as a NON-causal statement: 'More firefighters cause more fire damage.'
practice_problems.answer: 'Fires with more firefighters tend to have more damage' -- they are associated, but a bigger fire drives both.

practice_problems.stem: A plot shows a strong positive association between ice-cream sales and sunburns. A student says 'ice cream causes sunburns.' Is the claim justified?
practice_problems.answer: No -- hot, sunny weather increases both ice-cream sales and sunburns. The association does not prove ice cream causes sunburns.

practice_problems.stem: Create a set of (x, y) pairs (at least 6 points) with a negative, linear association and one outlier. List them.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 60), (2, 52), (3, 45), (4, 38), (5, 30), (6, 22) with an outlier at (3, 5). The bulk falls by about 8 each step; (3, 5) sits far below.

practice_problems.stem: A person made a scatter plot and wrote a description. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: They wrote: 'This shows that increasing x CAUSES y to drop.'
practice_problems.answer: The data does show a negative association (y falls as x rises), but a scatter plot cannot prove CAUSATION. The correct description is 'a negative, linear association,' not a cause-and-effect claim -- some other factor may drive both.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: sliding from association to causation.

practice_problems.stem: A person's plot rises and then bends upward more steeply. They call it 'positive, linear.' Critique and correct the description.
practice_problems.answer: The direction is right (positive), but the form is wrong: a bending path is nonlinear. The correct description is 'positive, nonlinear.'
practice_problems.notes: Critique a described pattern (matches the Above band).

practice_problems.stem: Create a scatter-plot description (a list of points) that a classmate must critique: include one true feature and one that is easy to over-claim as causation.
practice_problems.answer: Example: (1, 5), (2, 9), (3, 14), (4, 20), (5, 27) for 'hours of daylight vs ice-cream sales' -- a positive association, but claiming daylight CAUSES the sales ignores temperature as a hidden driver.

practice_problems.stem: Two variables show NO association. A student concludes 'so one prevents the other.' What is wrong with that?
practice_problems.answer: No association means the variables do not move together at all -- it gives no evidence that one prevents (or causes) the other. No pattern means no such conclusion.

activities.title: Justified or Overclaiming?
materials: Claim cards pairing a described plot with a statement
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Justified description' or 'Overclaims causation.'
2. For each 'overclaims' card, name a hidden variable that could explain both.
3. Rewrite each overclaiming card as a 'tend to move together' statement.
4. Debrief: which words (causes, makes, because of) are red flags on a scatter plot?

cards.text: Positive plot: 'x and y tend to increase together.'
Positive plot: 'x causes y to increase.'
Ice cream & sunburns rise together: 'ice cream causes sunburns.'
Negative plot: 'as x increases, y tends to decrease.'
Firefighters & damage rise together: 'more firefighters cause more damage.'
Curved rising plot: 'this is a positive, nonlinear association.'

activities.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
activities.instructions:
1. Read the claim that a negative association between x and y proves 'x causes y to drop.'
2. Underline the cause word and ask: does the plot show cause, or just that they move together?
3. Name a hidden variable that could drive both.
4. Rewrite the description without a cause claim, and write the rule: a scatter plot shows association, not causation.

content.worked_problem: (1, 90), (2, 72), (3, 58), (4, 40), (5, 25). Claim: 'increasing x CAUSES y to drop.'
content.error_step: The claim reads a negative association as proof of cause and effect.
content.why: The plot shows y falls as x rises -- a negative association -- but a scatter plot cannot prove causation; a hidden variable may drive both.

strategy_links.why: The correlation-implies-causation leap is a precise, baitable error; find-and-fix that hunts for a hidden variable corrects it.
A math-journal entry justifying or critiquing a claim builds the argument habit the standard tops out on.
Think-pair-share debating 'is this claim justified?' forces students to defend or critique inferences aloud with the data as evidence.

questioning_prompts: Does the plot show that the variables move together, or that one causes the other?
What hidden variable could explain both of these at once?
Is the described pattern (direction and form) actually correct for this data?
How would you rewrite the claim so it is justified by the plot?
Does your created plot match every descriptor -- direction, form, and each feature?

misconception_redirects.say: A scatter plot can only show that two things move together. Before claiming cause, ask 'could a hidden variable explain both?' If yes, say the variables are associated, not that one causes the other.
misconception_redirects.praise: You named the pattern as an association and questioned the cause -- that's honest analysis.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student builds a plot to match descriptors but leaves out one descriptor (e.g., makes it negative but forgets the outlier).
misconception_redirects.say: Check your plot against EVERY word in the description -- direction, form, and each named feature. Missing one means the plot doesn't match.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked your plot against all the descriptors -- direction, form, and the outlier -- so it fully matches.

quick_checks.prompt: Positive association between number of firefighters and fire damage. Claim: 'firefighters cause damage.' Justified?
quick_checks.look_for: No -- fire size drives both. Accepting the claim diagnoses treating correlation as causation.

quick_checks.prompt: Build a list of 6 points with a positive, nonlinear association. Show it.
quick_checks.look_for: Growing steps, e.g., (1,2),(2,5),(3,11),(4,20),(5,32),(6,47). A straight-line set means the student missed the nonlinear descriptor.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (describe more than one characteristic of a scatter plot at once) -- the synthesis workhorse that pulls together direction, form, and outliers, matched to the Approaching-band items. If they pass, push to S5 (construct and interpret in context) and S6 (analyze, critique, and build plots to match descriptors). If they fail, drop to S1 (identify the association as positive/negative/none) and S2 (classify the form as linear/nonlinear) to find where the description breaks. S3 (identify clustering and outliers) branches off as the feature-spotting skill that feeds the full description.
